vignette:
Leilani Makani, a sixty-five-year-old cybersecurity analyst who lost her husband three years ago, came to therapy six months after a car crash that nearly killed her. She had been driving home late from a security breach response when a driver ran a red light and T-boned her car. Leilani was trapped in the crumpled driver's side with a shattered steering wheel pressing against her ribs. The smell of gasoline and burning rubber filled the cabin, and the headlights of oncoming traffic flashed in her periphery like strobes. She remembers thinking her body was giving out-her ribs wouldn't expand, her legs wouldn't move-and then the other driver fled the scene, leaving her alone and pinned. Nothing about the aftermath felt fair; the man was never found, and Leilani was left with multiple fractures and a deep sense that the world had wronged her.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani found herself unable to trust her own body. What frightened her most was the feeling that other people could see what had happened just by looking at her face-that her trauma was written across her skin. These appraisals drove her to push away any emotion, positive or negative, because feeling anything reminded her how fragile she had become. She also began to go over and over why the accident had happened to her, as though finding an answer could undo the injustice. At the same time, she started scanning her environment for danger: she found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and she would wake several times to check that her apartment was secure. Leilani believed that staying alert was the only way to avoid another catastrophe-especially at night, when she struggled to fall asleep because she needed to remain vigilant. Her body, she had concluded, could not be trusted to protect her, so she had to do it herself.

The memories of the crash were not just thoughts; they arrived as vivid pictures-the glare of oncoming headlights, the way the dashboard crumpled-and sometimes she would smell gasoline out of nowhere, even in her own home. Worse, when the memory surfaced, she felt a sharp pain in her ribs exactly where they had been fractured, as though the accident were happening again. These sensory intrusions always heightened her sense of hypervigilance: every creak of the building or distant siren became a potential threat, and she would lie rigid in bed, scanning the dark. The more alert she became at night, the more her memory seemed to intrude-as if the act of checking her safety triggered the visual images and the smell of fuel. And each time that happened, the injustice burned hotter: she would ask herself why she had been the one left injured and abandoned.

Leilani tried to erase the memory of the event, but the effort only made the pictures and the phantom ache in her ribs return more vividly. She avoided any reminder of the crash-though she could not avoid the work she still needed to do as a cybersecurity analyst, now from home because she refused to drive. At night, she would check her system alerts obsessively, partly because a flagged intrusion gave her a focus that was not the accident, but the vigilance itself kept her memory alive: the glow of the monitor at 3 a.m. reminded her of the headlights, and she would smell gasoline again, her ribs throbbing. The cycle tightened. Her avoidance of all feelings meant she never talked about the crash, but her rumination about the injustice occupied hours of her sleep and kept her threat system online. She had come to believe that if she stopped scanning the dark for danger, something terrible would happen again-and that certainty made her night vigil feel necessary even as it exhausted her.

What finally brought Leilani into the clinic was a comment from her daughter, who noticed she had stopped eating with the family and never left the apartment. Leilani's primary hope was simply to stop the smell of gasoline from appearing when she tried to rest. But what she was most afraid of was that if she let her guard down-even for a moment-her body would fail her again, and this time she might not survive.
